How does each site compare to its seasonal normal?
Why this matters for West Boundary agriculture

Summer is when agricultural water demand peaks and natural supply is lowest. The West Boundary has faced repeated drought stress, including the 2021 Temporary Protection Order in the West Kettle watershed that restricted withdrawals.

The envelope chart and the comparisons above put today’s flows in the context of decades of record (48–70 years per main station), so producers and planners can quickly see whether the watershed is tracking toward a low-flow year. When the red line sits near or below the lower edge of the blue band, the watershed is running drier than usual for the season — an early signal for storage, conservation, and engagement decisions.

Long-term trend — summer low flow (7-day minimum, Jul–Sep)
What the trend means

The 7-day summer low flow is the metric regulators and drought planners watch most closely — it captures the sustained low-water conditions that stress irrigation and aquatic habitat.

A declining long-term trend in summer lows is consistent with warmer summers, earlier snowmelt, and increasing water demand in the West Boundary. It does not predict any single year, but it frames why storage, efficiency, and cooperative planning matter even in non-drought years.

Why snowpack matters here

Grano Creek (2E07P) is the Boundary Region’s only real-time automated snow station in the Kettle River watershed. Snow that accumulates at elevation is the reservoir that feeds spring freshet and summer baseflow — low or early-melting snowpack is a leading indicator that summer irrigation supply may be tight, often months before streamflow hits critical levels.

The RDKB drought updates and provincial snow bulletins use this station to track whether the watershed entered the growing season with adequate mountain storage.

Why groundwater matters here

The Kettle valley aquifers are strongly connected to the river — the Grand Forks aquifer sits next to the Kettle/Granby confluence and rises and falls with the freshet. When both streamflow and water tables are running below normal at the same time, it points to a basin-wide moisture deficit rather than a local blip — an important signal for irrigation timing, storage, and shared conservation decisions.

What this dashboard is

A pilot dashboard for the RDKB West Boundary Agricultural Water Supply and Storage planning process. It brings public hydrometric information together in an accessible place to support planning and community engagement — helping producers, First Nations, local government, and agencies share a common picture of seasonal water conditions and drought risk in the Kettle River watershed from Midway upstream.

It is not a regulatory monitoring tool. Readings are provisional and unverified, and should not be used for compliance or enforcement.

Data sources & methods
  • Live streamflow: Environment and Climate Change Canada (ECCC) real-time hydrometric web service, retrieved with the open-source tidyhydat R package (parameter 47, daily mean, m³/s).
  • Streamflow normals: Water Survey of Canada HYDAT database, precomputed by scripts/build_flow_normals.R and scripts/build_flow_analytics.R (MAD thresholds, drought analog years, summer low-flow trend).
  • Groundwater: B.C. Provincial Groundwater Observation Well Network (PGOWN), precomputed by scripts/build_gw_normals.R.
  • Snowpack: B.C. Automated Snow Weather Station Grano Creek (2E07P) via the B.C. Data Catalogue (scripts/build_snow_normals.R).
  • Status classes: Severe Low (least water available — below the 10th percentile for the day), then Low, Normal, Above Normal, High.
Confidentiality & responsible use

This dashboard uses public and voluntarily shared information only. Should producer-contributed inputs (for example well levels, repeat photo points, or irrigation timing) be added in future, they would be aggregated or anonymised so that individual operations cannot be identified, consistent with the project’s commitment to a transparent, non-regulatory process and with FOIPPA.

Ownership, hosting & upkeep

Built entirely with open-source tools (Quarto + R) so it can be fully owned, hosted, and maintained by the Regional District. All source files, data-build scripts, and documentation are included in the project repository. Refreshing the historical baselines is a single command (Rscript scripts/build_flow_normals.R); live readings update automatically each time the site is rebuilt.

Potential future inputs identified in the RFP — groundwater well levels, date-stamped/repeat photo points, and irrigation season timing — can be added as additional pages using the same pattern.
